2104044508170358874 The_AI_Investor Samsung is about to report the biggest quarter in its history. Analysts now expect Q3 operating profit of 106T to 110T won, per Aju Press on Sept 27 KST. For perspective, Samsung earned 43.6T won in all of last year, so one quarter would be nearly two and a half times the entire 2025. No quarter has ever crossed 100T before.  The driver is memory, plain and simple. TrendForce estimates Q3 DRAM and NAND prices rose about 10% to the mid high teens from Q2. That pace is slower than Q2's roughly 60% spike, but AI demand is strong enough that prices kept climbing. Since chipmakers' costs barely move when prices rise, the DS division's operating margin could reach the mid 70% range, with DRAM alone above 80%. HBM4 is adding to it: Samsung's HBM market share jumped to 33% in Q2.  Everything else lags. Foundry and System LSI are still expected to lose about 1T won combined. So this record quarter is a memory story, full stop. Industry sources expect the tight supply to last at least into 2028. 

2103987326460498098 PatrickMoorhead On Tuesday at the @GlobalSemi US Executive Forum in Menlo Park, I moderated "Silicon at the Breaking Point: Designing Chips for a World That Can't Wait" with @SamsungDSGlobal President Paul Cho, @AMD CTO Mark Papermaster, @Broadcom Semiconductor Solutions Group President Charlie Kawwas and @OpenAI VP of Hardware Richard Ho.   The lead-in was that the transistor is no longer the bottleneck. Power, memory bandwidth and packaging are. I opened with that, and not one of the four pushed back. Each built on it from his first answer.  On custom silicon: Richard framed OpenAI's XPU as a full-stack bet on intelligence per watt for a known set of workloads, not a bet against merchant GPUs. The unit of purchase is now the fleet across multiple campuses, not the chip or the rack. I said years ago that 75+% design margins would push the biggest buyers to find another path. They found it. Charlie's outlook is single campuses of 5 to 10 gigawatts by 2031.  On power: Mark's line was that power is performance, and data movement is where most of it goes. Chiplets were a power decision at AMD before anything else. Thermal and cooling are now job one.  On AI in the design loop: Richard said AI compressed OpenAI's design cycle more than his team expected, and the point is to make engineers faster, not to replace them. Mark's rule at AMD is that agentic AI runs the design space exploration no human could do by hand, and accountability stays with the human engineer. I agree with both.  On packaging: Charlie called the substrate the choke point for the next five years, which is why Broadcom is going into substrate production itself. On the OpenAI program, Broadcom's tape-out went from 15 to 18 months to nine. His math: that cadence is an extra generation every three years, and in AI that is the whole game.  On memory: Paul had the stat of the night. By his numbers, compute is up roughly 60,000x in 20 years and memory bandwidth roughly 100x. Design memory first and bring the memory partner into architecture, not procurement. He also said supply chain resilience is now a design input decided at architecture definition, and that Samsung's Taylor, Texas fab goes to customer mass production in 2027.  The node still delivers, at a price. The advantage now goes to whoever co-designs compute, memory, packaging, networking and power from day one. That is structural, not a phase. $AMD $AVGO   Thanks to all four for the candor, and to the GSA team led by Jodi Shelton and Cherie Britt at Samsung for pulling it together. Several points are worth putting on the record. 

2103855583485165741 The_AI_Investor COHR LITE. Washington just handed US optics a demand tailwind. Senators Cornyn, McCormick, Fetterman and Gallego introduced bipartisan legislation to bar optical transceivers from Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight in sensitive US national security systems. Optical transceivers are the modules that convert electrical signals into light pulses to move data between servers, and large AI data centers need millions of them.  The bill gives the government five years to comply and lets the Commerce and Defense secretaries add more Chinese vendors to the list. The industry pushback is already on the record: the ITI wrote the FCC in August warning that supply disruption would slow US data center deployment, and Reuters reports Coherent and Lumentum sell competitive technology but lack the scale to replace Chinese vendors today.  The government slice of transceiver demand is small, but the signal matters more than the volume. If federal procurement goes domestic first, the same logic spreads to hyperscaler supply chains worried about firmware risk in reprogrammable transceivers. Coherent is the prime beneficiary by position, the risk is that Western capacity cannot scale fast enough and the buildout slows instead.
